newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Gulf Coast braces for tropical storm.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Gulf Coast braces for tropical storm.

text.p: People along the U.S. Gulf Coast braced on Thursday for high winds and heavy rains as slow-moving Tropical Storm Danny lumbered toward shore.
Officials warned residents of Louisiana and Mississippi that the storm, with winds of up to 60 miles per hour (96 kph), could flood low-lying areas as it moved in from the Gulf of Mexico.

The National Hurricane Centre in Miami said rains from Danny were already pelting the Lousiana coast. It said the storm could strengthen before hitting land, and it issued a hurricane watch that stretched from Cameron, La. to Orange Beach, Ala.
Rains of five to 10 inches (13 to 25 cm) could accompany the storm, it said.

Danny's centre was 115 miles (185 kph) southwest of New Orleans and moving northeast at about 5 mph (8 kph). The eye of the storm was expected to make landfall late on Thursday or early on Friday, the hurricane centre said.

Marshall Wickman, meteorologist for Houston-based private forecaster Wilkens Weather Technologies, told Reuters that Danny was likely to come ashore near Port Fourchon, La., 60 miles (96 km) south of New Orleans.
A spokesman for the Louisiana Office of Emergency Preparedness said state officials were not expecting major damage from the storm, but coastal residents were on alert.
"Right now, you could say we're in the first stage of monitoring, where we kind of sit up and lean forward a bit," spokesman Brett Kriger said.
U.S. Coast Guard spokesman Ron Mench said the Coast Guard was "gearing up and warning people that if you're out on a small boat it's time to get off the water and come on in."
Offshore oil producing platforms were battered overnight by heavy winds and high waves. Some companies began taking workers off the rigs and bringing them ashore.
"We're pulling about 100 non-operating personnel off various rigs and platforms," Texaco Inc. spokesman Pierre DeGruy said.
So far, he said, the storm had not forced the platforms to shut down. "We're on standby-alert status on other platforms, but no production is shut in," DeGruy said.
The storm was upgraded to a tropical storm on Thursday when its sustained winds reached 39 mph (63 kph). It would become a hurricane if its winds climb to 74 mph (119 kph).
